lessons.title: Anatomy of the horse
lessons.html:
Why anatomy comes first

Conformation is the shape and structure of a horse: how its bones, muscles and joints are put together. To judge conformation you must first know the parts of the horse and what lies underneath them.

Points of the horse

RegionPoints
Head and neckPoll, forelock, forehead, muzzle, nostril, jaw (jowl), throat, crest, neck
ForehandWithers, shoulder, point of shoulder, chest, elbow, forearm, knee, cannon, fetlock, pastern, coronet, hoof
BodyBack, loins, ribs (barrel), girth, belly, flank
HindquartersCroup, point of hip, dock, buttock, thigh, stifle, gaskin, hock, point of hock, hind cannon, fetlock, pastern, hoof

The skeleton

  • Skull and neck: the neck has seven vertebrae and acts as a balancing arm for the horse.
  • Spine: neck (cervical), back (thoracic, carrying the ribs), loins (lumbar), croup (sacral, fused) and tail vertebrae. The withers are formed by the tall spines of the first thoracic vertebrae.
  • Forelimb: the horse has no collarbone; the forelimb is attached to the body only by muscles and ligaments. Bones: shoulder blade (scapula), humerus, radius (forearm), knee (carpus, the equivalent of the human wrist), cannon bone with splint bones, fetlock joint, long and short pastern bones, coffin bone inside the hoof.
  • Hindlimb: pelvis, femur, stifle (equivalent of the human knee, with the patella), tibia (gaskin), hock (tarsus, equivalent of the human ankle), cannon, fetlock, pastern and coffin bones.

Muscles, tendons and ligaments

Below the knee and hock there are no muscles, only tendons and ligaments. The flexor tendons run down the back of the cannon, and the suspensory ligament supports the fetlock. These structures carry huge loads at speed and are commonly injured when conformation puts extra strain on them.

Movement

The hindquarters are the "engine" that pushes the horse forward. The forelegs carry about 60% of the horse's weight at rest and absorb impact. Good conformation lets the limbs move straight and the joints share the load evenly.

lessons.title: Recognising correct conformation
lessons.html:
How to assess a horse

  1. Stand the horse on firm, level ground, standing square (all four legs evenly under it).
  2. Look from a distance first at the overall picture, then move closer.
  3. Look from the left side, the front, the right side and from behind.
  4. Watch the horse walk and trot towards you, away from you and from the side on a hard surface.
  5. Feel the legs for lumps, heat or old injuries.

Overall balance and proportion

  • From the side, the body can be divided into three roughly equal parts: shoulder (forehand), barrel (middle) and hindquarters.
  • Height at the withers and at the croup should be about the same in a mature horse.
  • The back should be relatively short and strong, with well-muscled loins.
  • Body length and height are roughly in proportion; the horse should fit into a square or a slightly longer rectangle depending on the breed.
  • The head should be in proportion to the body and well attached at the throat.
  • The neck should come out of the shoulders with a gentle upward curve along the top.

The forelegs

  • A sloping shoulder gives a longer stride and absorbs shock.
  • From the front, a vertical line from the point of shoulder should divide the forearm, knee, cannon, fetlock and hoof in half.
  • From the side, a vertical line from the middle of the forearm should run down through the knee and fetlock to the back of the heel.
  • Knees are large, flat and level; cannons short and strong.
  • The pastern slopes at about the same angle as the front of the hoof.

The hindlegs

  • From the side, a vertical line from the point of buttock should touch the point of the hock and run down the back of the cannon to the ground.
  • From behind, a vertical line from the point of buttock should divide the hock, cannon, fetlock and hoof in half.
  • Hocks are large, clean and well-defined; the gaskin is well muscled.

Feet

Feet should be a matching pair in front and a matching pair behind, of a size that suits the horse, with a good depth of heel and a wide frog.

lessons.title: Conformation defects and their effects
lessons.html:
Common defects

DefectDescriptionEffect on performance
Ewe neckTop line of neck dips, bulge underneathHarder to balance and accept the bit; head carried high
Upright shoulderShoulder angle steepShorter, choppy stride; more concussion on the forelegs
Long backBack long in relation to the bodyWeaker back, harder to engage the hindquarters; more back strain
Sway (hollow) backBack dips markedlySaddle fitting problems, weakness; common in old horses
Back at the knee (calf knees)Knee behind the vertical line when seen from the sideStrain on the knee and flexor tendons; high risk in racehorses
Over at the kneeKnee in front of the vertical lineUsually less serious; may stumble
Tied in below the kneeCannon narrower just below the kneeWeak tendon support; tendon injuries
Offset (bench) kneesCannon set to the outside of the kneeExtra stress on the inside of the leg; splints
Toes in (pigeon toes) / toes outFeet turn in or outPaddling or winging; uneven loading of joints; brushing injuries with toes out
Long, sloping pasternsPasterns low and longStrain on tendons and suspensory ligament
Short, upright pasternsPasterns steep and shortMore concussion; risk of joint and foot problems
Sickle hocksToo much angle in the hock; cannon slopes forwardStrain on the back of the hock (curb)
Straight (post) hocksToo little angleConcussion; stifle and hock problems
Cow hocksHocks point in towards each otherUneven stress on the hock joints
Small or mismatched feetFeet too small for body, or different shapesConcussion, lameness; may indicate an old problem

Judging how serious a defect is

No horse is perfect. Ask three questions:

  1. How severe is it? A slight deviation matters less than a marked one.
  2. What will the horse be used for? Back at the knee is serious in a racehorse or jumper, but less important in a light hack.
  3. Has it caused damage already? Look for splints, windgalls, curbs or uneven hoof wear.

Some defects in foals improve with growth; others can be helped by correct trimming. Some faults are inherited, so conformation is important when selecting breeding stock.

Key points

  • Know the points of the horse and the skeleton beneath them.
  • Assess on level ground, standing square, from all sides and in movement.
  • Use vertical lines to check straight leg alignment from front, side and behind.
  • Defects such as back at the knee, tied in, and sickle hocks increase injury risk.
  • Judge defects by severity, the horse's intended use, and evidence of damage.
